query: I am investigating a quaternary equiatomic alloy with a face-centered cubic (FCC) structure, specifically looking for the relationship between its mechanical properties and its corrosion resistance. What hypotheses can be proposed regarding the plastic deformation mechanisms under uniaxial tension? Please provide supporting prior evidence for dislocation-based yielding, identify the boundary conditions where yield strength might become insensitive to strain rate, and propose a falsification experiment to distinguish between dislocation glide and phase transformation mechanisms.

generation.hypothesis: In quaternary equiatomic FCC alloys, plastic deformation under uniaxial tension is primarily governed by dislocation glide at intermediate to high temperatures (>300 K), while at cryogenic temperatures, deformation twinning and FCC-HCP phase transformations become dominant mechanisms, leading to enhanced strength and ductility. Yield strength becomes insensitive to strain rate at temperatures above 800 K where diffusion-controlled mechanisms (dislocation climb, grain boundary sliding) dominate over athermal dislocation glide.
generation.material_initial_state: Quaternary equiatomic face-centered cubic (FCC) solid solution alloy with homogeneous composition and single-phase structure, containing elements such as Co, Cr, Fe, Ni (or similar FCC-stabilizing elements).
generation.intervention: Uniaxial tensile deformation applied at varying temperatures (77 K to 1273 K) and strain rates (10^-4 to 10^2 s^-1) to probe deformation mechanisms.
generation.conditions: Temperature range: 77 K to 1273 K; Strain rates: 10^-4 to 10^2 s^-1; Vacuum or inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation; Single-phase FCC microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: Dislocation structures (cell structures, wavy/zigzag dislocations), deformation twins, and FCC-HCP phase transformation interfaces that evolve with temperature and strain.
generation.mechanism: At low temperatures (<300 K), deformation is dominated by twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) and transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) due to hindered dislocation motion from chemical short-range order and lattice friction. At high temperatures (>800 K), diffusion-controlled mechanisms (dislocation climb, grain boundary sliding) dominate, reducing strain rate sensitivity. The transition between mechanisms is mediated by thermal activation of dislocation glide and twin boundary mobility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Yield strength increases with decreasing temperature due to enhanced TWIP/TRIP effects. Strain rate sensitivity decreases significantly above 800 K. Ductility peaks at cryogenic temperatures due to delayed necking from twinning. Phase transformations (FCC to HCP) occur at low temperatures and high strains, contributing to work hardening.
generation.baseline: Conventional FCC alloys (e.g., pure metals or binary alloys) where dislocation glide is the primary mechanism across all temperatures, with minimal twinning or phase transformation contributions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to single-phase FCC equiatomic alloys with moderate to high stacking fault energy. It may not hold for multi-phase alloys, BCC structures, or alloys with very low stacking fault energy where martensitic transformation dominates.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature threshold for mechanism transition may vary depending on specific alloy composition and stacking fault energy. The role of chemical short-range order in hindering dislocation motion is not fully quantified for all quaternary systems. Strain rate insensitivity at high temperatures may be influenced by grain size and texture.
generation.falsification_experiment: Perform in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction during uniaxial tensile testing at cryogenic (77 K) and high temperatures (1000 K) to directly observe the evolution of crystal structure. If dislocation glide is the dominant mechanism at all temperatures, no FCC-HCP phase transformation or significant twinning should be detected. Conversely, if phase transformation or twinning dominates at low temperatures, diffraction peaks corresponding to HCP phase or twin-related peak splitting should appear. Additionally, measure yield strength at multiple strain rates at 800 K; if yield strength remains constant across strain rates, it confirms diffusion-controlled dominance, whereas significant strain rate dependence would falsify the insensitivity hypothesis.

Microstructure of selective laser-melted equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy

Figure 1 shows an SEM-BSE image and EDS mapping results of as-built equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA. The BSE image revealed some micron-scale gas pores, but coarse defects or cracks were not observed in the as-built HEA (Porosity: 0.13%). The density of the present alloy was measured as 7.96 g/cm 3 which was similar to that of the theoretical density of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA. In addition, Co, Cr, Fe, Mn, and Ni were all around 20 at. % in EDS mapping analysis, and all elements were evenly distributed. Li et al . [38] found that Mn undergoes segregation when equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA is manufactured using SLM. According to Wang et al . [41] , when equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA was manufactured with pre-alloyed powder using electron beam melting (EBM), it was confirmed that Fe, Cr and Co elements segregate into the dendrite, whereas, Mn and Ni segregate into the interdendrite region. However, when the optimal process condition using SLM was deduced, no dendritic microstructure was formed, and it was possible to manufacture a random solid solution HEA with compositional homogeneity.

3.1. Deformation Behavior of Ag NWs and CoNiCrFeMn HEA NWs

Figure 2 shows the stress–strain curves of the Ag NWs and CoNiCrFeMn HEA NWs at 77, 300, and 1000 K respectively. At 77 K, Ag NW deforms via nucleation and propagation of a partial dislocation from the free surface, leaving a stacking fault inside the NW (see Figure 3 a). As deformation continues, the stacking fault further separates into two twin boundaries, which extend and continue to grow through entire NW. The cross-section area of the NW eventually converts from (110) to (100), resulting in two peaks in the SS curve, as shown in Figure 2 a. The area between two twin boundaries is transformed as also shown in Figure 3 a between 8% to 32% elongation in the Ag NW. The phase transformation is mainly driven by the surface stresses which enable the reduction in surface energy in the nanowire. On further loading, the difference between two boundaries decreases and finally vanishes at around 50% elongation, resulting in an improved work hardening. Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
